newsitem.title: JAPAN: INTERVIEW-TGE plans arabica/robusta coffee futures.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-TGE plans arabica/robusta coffee futures.

text.p: The president of the Tokyo Grain Exchange (TGE) said on Friday that the exchange will offer both arabica and robusta coffee once it launches a yen-based coffee futures contract.
In March, the TGE set up a committee to study the listing of a coffee futures contract and aims to finalise details by this September.
"Japan is a major consumer of both arabica and robusta coffee, and I think it makes great sense to list both brands simultaneously here," president Takao Morizane told Reuters.

Japan, the world's third largest consumer of coffee after the United States and Germany, imported 326,388 tonnes of green coffee in calendar 1996, mainly from Brazil, Colombia and Indonesia, Finance Ministry data showed.
"The New York market trades arabica coffee, while the London market lists robusta. If we can trade both brands, TGE will be an unique market for the world coffee industry," Morizane said.
The idea of launching a yen-based coffee futures contract first sprang up in 1987, but plans have been on hold due mainly to opposition from the local coffee industry.
Morizane said the TGE is having unofficial talks with local industry officials on listing the new contracts. "At this stage I can't tell exactly when we can start trading," he said.
The TGE president also said that the exchange is considering listing soyoil and soymeal contracts.
Japan imported nearly 4.87 million tonnes of soybeans last year, mainly from the United States, Finance Ministry data showed.
The beans are processed in Japan into soyoil and soymeal, which are mainly used for making edible oil and feed.
"Trading of soyoil and soymeal in Asia is growing, for example in China. So I think it makes sense to launch the futures contracts for them," Morizane said. He did not elaborate further.

TGE's trading volume in 1996 hit a record high of 27.51 million lots, up by 87.8 percent from the previous year, due to volatile grain markets. Of that, corn futures' volume reached a record high of 16.03 million lots, more than double the 6.89 million lots in 1995.
Industry officials say the TGE's growing profile is increasingly becoming a concern for the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT), which is the centre of world grain trading,
Asked about that, Morizane said: "I'm aware of CBOT's concern. But we're just trying to meet the needs of customers in Japan and neighbouring countries.
"We have no ambition to take over Chicago's position."
